bottle.name: Hennessy Very Special Cognac

records.table: Hennessy Very Special is the young cognac of Hennessy, the house an Irish officer founded in Cognac in 1765, blended from some forty eaux-de-vie of four crus. Toast, almond and brown sugar make it a cognac for neat sipping, a ginger ale highball or a Sidecar.
records.story: Richard Hennessy (1724 to 1800), born in County Cork, served the French king in the Irish Brigade, then settled in Cognac and founded a trading house for its eaux-de-vie in 1765. His son built the business and brought in a family of blenders, the Fillioux, whose sons followed their fathers into the role for generations. By the house's account every eau-de-vie it uses is tasted by its committee before it goes into a blend. In 1865, by the house's own account, the family helped bring in grading by stars, and the Three Star cognac of that system is the line that the V.S of the label carries on. In 1971 Hennessy merged with the Champagne house Moët et Chandon to form Moët Hennessy, and in 1987 Moët Hennessy merged with Louis Vuitton to form LVMH. For a bartender the V.S is the bottle a guest names when he asks for cognac by brand, and the plainest lesson in what the grade letters promise: a floor of two years in oak, not an age.

records.story: In 1724 a young vine grower from near Rouillac set up a cognac trading house under his own name, by the house's account, and the business stayed with his family for generations. In 1924 André Renaud (died 1965) took charge of the house and became, by its account, its first cellar master. In 1927 he launched the VSOP Fine Champagne, a blend drawn only from the two chalky crus at the heart of the region, and in 1938 the Fine Champagne appellation was recognised in law. When Renaud died in 1965, his son-in-law took over the firm. In 1990 the holding companies of Rémy Martin and of Cointreau, the orange liqueur house of Angers, merged, and in 1991 the group took the name Rémy Cointreau. The house kept its rule of blending from the two Champagne crus alone. For a bartender this one bottle teaches two label words at once: what VSOP promises about age, and what Fine Champagne means about origin, which has nothing to do with sparkling wine.

records.table: Martell Cordon Bleu is the extra old cognac of Martell, the house a merchant from Jersey founded in Cognac in 1715, built around old eaux-de-vie of the Borderies. Candied plum, mocha and toasted almond make it a cognac to sip neat at room temperature.
records.story: Jean Martell (1694 to 1753), born at St Brelade in Jersey, set up as a merchant of eaux-de-vie in Cognac, on the Charente, in 1715. His descendants built a house style on the Borderies, a small cru whose eaux-de-vie are round and floral, and on clear wine distilled without its lees. In 1912 the founder's great-grandson created Cordon Bleu, an extra old cognac given a name of its own; by the house's account it was launched at the Hôtel de Paris in Monaco. The blend, of more than a hundred eaux-de-vie, has kept its name and its Borderies heart ever since. The family ran the firm for most of three centuries. Seagram bought the house in 1988, and Pernod Ricard acquired it with Seagram's drinks business in 2001. For a bartender Cordon Bleu is the bottle that teaches the Borderies: ask what a cru brings to a blend, and this is the answer to pour, beside the house's arched XO decanter.

records.table: Courvoisier VSOP is the four-cru cognac of Courvoisier, the house of Jarnac on the Charente, aged up to twelve years in its own oak. Stone fruit, toasted almond and gingerbread make it a cognac built for a Sidecar or a Vieux Carré.
records.story: Courvoisier dates itself to 1828. By the house's account a Paris wine and spirits firm at Bercy, run by the founder's father and a partner, passed to their sons, who set up a second company at Jarnac on the Charente; the house's own building there followed in 1857. The house tells that the emperor Napoléon III (1808 to 1873) named it a supplier to his court, and a legend says he inherited the taste from his uncle: a story the brand has kept on its labels as the cognac of Napoléon. Félix Courvoisier (died 1866) left no heir, and the house passed to his nephews. In 1909 the Simon family, wine and spirits merchants in Britain, took over the firm and, by one account, gave it the slogan the Brandy of Napoléon. The house changed hands several times in the century that followed, and in 2024 Campari bought it from Beam Suntory. For a bartender the VSOP is the working cognac of the house: four crus, a round, fruity middle, and enough body to carry citrus in a Sidecar.

records.table: Ferrand 1840 Original Formula is the Grande Champagne cognac Ferrand blended at 45 per cent after a bottle of 1840 made for mixing. Ripe grape, honey and spice stand up in a Sidecar, a julep or a Vieux Carré.
records.story: The Ferrand name comes from a family of growers at Ségonzac, in Grande Champagne, where ten generations of its men, each named Elie, worked the vines and stills over three centuries, by the house's account. The family built its manor there in 1861, and the male line ended in 1915, when the tenth of them died of wounds from the First World War. In 1989 a new firm, Maison Ferrand, was founded to revive the name, and by its account the Château de Bonbonnet at Ars became the heart of its work. In 2011 the house released 1840 Original Formula, made with its cellar master and a drinks historian to recreate the three star cognac that bartenders of the nineteenth century poured into punches, juleps and crustas. The blend was modelled closely on a well-kept bottle of Pinet-Castillon cognac from 1840, and it is bottled at 45 per cent, above the 40 of most young cognacs, so that it keeps its fruit once it meets ice and sugar. For a bartender it is the cognac made to answer the old recipes as their authors wrote them.
